items.title: Human-AI Collaboration in Urban Digital Transformation: Balancing Efficiency and Human Values in Shanghai’s AI-Enabled Talent Recruitment
items.abstract: In the context of the urban digital revolution, recruitment through AI technologies has become common practice to address competition in the labor market. However, it is still unclear how the effectiveness of such recruitment is connected with humanistic values. For this research, an exploratory qualitative research design was used, involving semi-structured interviews with eight human resource professionals in Shanghai. Based on the results, the use of AI in recruitment led to increased efficiency mainly when screening candidates through high-volume, standardized processes, although the promised efficiency was not delivered in practice because the introduction of the AI system increased the workload. Patterns of human-machine cooperation were observed in different companies: tech companies and foreign companies are inclined to adopt interactive adjustment approaches, while state-owned enterprises retain human-dominated decision-making. Transparency of algorithms was still lacking in numerous instances, and there was an asymmetry in the accountability framework of algorithms, wherein disobeying algorithms carries more personal consequences than obeying them. The more experienced professionals became more autonomous in their work, while the less experienced professionals depended more on the algorithm. Issues like management support, information accuracy, and departmental integration have a major impact on implementation. This study contributes to the theory of human-machine collaboration by proposing the concept of asymmetric algorithmic accountability, which captures the uneven distribution of organizational consequences for following versus overriding AI recommendations and shapes practitioner behavior in ways that extend beyond individual trust or algorithmic transparency.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

items.title: Identification and control of potential occupational safety and health hazards of artificial intelligence: a scoping review
items.abstract: Introduction Artificial intelligence (AI) offers substantial societal benefits, but it also can pose significant hazards to workers. Methods A scoping literature review was conducted to identify materials published from 2010 to 2025 and indicative of artificial intelligence (AI) hazards to workers. The aim was to answer two research questions: What are the potential occupational safety and health hazards associated with exposure to AI? and What are the approaches that have been proposed to control these hazards in the workplace? Results Eight databases and grey literature were searched. These yielded 25,925 studies, which after screening resulted in 622 studies for full text review. Of these, 216 were eligible for data extraction. These studies substantiated 14 categories of potential hazards to workers from AI. These categories included: threats of physical trauma; dehumanization of workers; threats to human agency, autonomy, and workers’ voice; loss of human and workplace connection; threats to sense of self and identity; threats of increased stress, fatigue, and work-life imbalance from work intensification; dependence on AI, leading to deterioration of skills; potential exacerbation of OSH inequities in the workplace; threats of weakening the psychological contract, worker engagement, and trust; threats of job loss, unemployment, disruption of labor market, and reduced economic mobility; threats of underpaid, precarious, and hidden work; threats of cyberphysical attacks and bullying; inappropriate worker monitoring, surveillance, management, and selection; and threats of adverse consequences of worker cognitive and physical augmentation and enhancement. Control approaches also were identified for each hazard category. Discussion This study provides a comprehensive appraisal of AI-related potential OSH hazards and controls and offers a foundation for future research and practice.

items.title: Impact Matters! Overview of the development and application process of the Impact AI Method: a holistic impact assessment for running AI projects
items.abstract: The overall rapid increase in the use of artificial intelligence technologies (AIT) is linked to various initiatives that propose AI ‘for good’. However, a holistic, in-depth understanding of these AI use cases and their implications for people, society, and the planet remains lacking, beyond the respective projects’ self-descriptions. To close this gap, we present a framework for a holistic yet manageable approach for running AI projects to assess their impact. We call our approach the Impact AI Method, as we not only want to assess the impacts of AI use cases but also want to impact AI and its use in practice and in public debate. The Impact AI Method evaluates concrete AI use cases in terms of their contribution to sustainability and public interest, reflecting these two concepts as well as established international guiding principles such as democratic values and human rights. The interview- and survey-based methodological approach combines and extends existing assessment approaches, incorporating a catalogue of 25 assessment criteria to evaluate the results. The Impact AI Method is intended as a reusable blueprint to inform public debate about AI ‘for good’ claims and to support the creation of evidence and transparency for AI systems that purport to contribute to just and sustainable development.

items.title: Implementation Challenges of Artificial Intelligence-Empowered Project-Based Learning in Compulsory Education
items.abstract: With the rapid development of generative artificial intelligence, new possibilities have emerged for addressing problems in project-based learning at the compulsory education stage, such as insufficient teacher guidance resources and inadequate personalized support for students. Based on literature research, this paper analyzes the implementation challenges faced by artificial intelligence-empowered project-based learning from the dual perspectives of teachers and students. The study finds that, at the teacher level, there are three types of problems: superficial AI application, generalized technology embedding, and fragmented instructional design. At the student level, there are difficulties such as the substitution of the inquiry process, interference with learning engagement, and compression of the space for collaborative construction. In response to these problems, this paper proposes optimization strategies, including promoting subject-differentiated technical support, designing structured collaborative learning sheets, improving the formative evaluation system, and enhancing teachers’ AI literacy, with a view to providing references for the deep integration of artificial intelligence and project-based learning in compulsory education.

items.title: Inteligencia artificial en enfermería: Percepción de los estudiantes sobre sus beneficios, riesgos y utilidad para la práctica profesional. Búsqueda narrativa
items.abstract: This article analyzes nursing students' perceptions regarding the benefits, risks, and utility of artificial intelligence (AI) in their academic training and future professional practice. Through a narrative review of scientific literature published between 2020 and August 2026, the study examines AI's educational and clinical applications. The results reveal a generally favorable perception of AI, driven by its speed, accessibility, and ability to simplify complex concepts, summarize information, and facilitate autonomous learning. Furthermore, these tools can support clinical reasoning, case development, and the preparation of academic activities. However, risks are identified regarding incorrect information, algorithmic bias, privacy, academic integrity, technological dependence, and a potential decline in critical thinking. These concerns highlight the need to develop the digital, ethical, and professional competencies required to use these tools responsibly. The study concludes that the integration of AI into nursing must be planned, supervised, and person-centered. It is essential to verify information, protect data, and preserve clinical judgment, ensuring that technology complements but never replaces humanized care and the professional responsibility of nursing staff.

items.title: Learner agency in GenAI-supported EFL academic writing under conditions of teacher trust
items.abstract: Learner agency in L2 academic writing has taken on new significance with the rapid uptake of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) tools, raising questions about how agency is exercised in interaction with these tools and what pedagogical conditions support agentic and learning-oriented use. This study examined how 27 Japanese undergraduates in a 14-week English academic writing course exercised agency across three AI-permitted out-of-class essays, and how that agency related to the development of their unassisted writing. The course was designed around a pedagogical stance of teacher trust with two named elements: discretion granted to learners over their AI use, and a structure of explicit guidelines, AI literacy instruction, articulated principles, and weekly group discussions. Post-writing reflections (n = 81) were coded for the function of tool use and the quality of agency across seven facets, with substantial inter-rater reliability for both. Computational indices of lexical diversity, lexical sophistication, syntactic complexity, and accuracy were extracted from in-class AI-free pre- and post-essays, and Turnitin AI detection scores were recorded as research data, not as a policing instrument. Individual facets of agency were associated with different aspects of unassisted writing development: metacognitive awareness with differences in length, learning orientation with gains in lexical diversity, and critical evaluation with gains in clause density. Composite agency was not associated with development on any measure, supporting a dimensional view of agency in which facets carry different consequences for learning. Unassisted writing also shifted toward shorter, less subordinated clauses across the semester, a direction conventional measures of L2 syntactic development were not designed to detect. The findings support a view in which trust as a pedagogical condition shapes the forms of agency available to learners.

items.title: Martabat Manusia di Era Digital: Interpretasi Ajaran Sosial Gereja terhadap Dampak Kecerdasan Buatan dalam Pendidikan
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has transformed the educational landscape through personalized learning, automated assessment, and expanded access to information; however, it has simultaneously raised ethical issues such as cognitive dependency, the erosion of academic integrity, algorithmic bias, digital attachment, and the weakening of pedagogical relationships. This study aims to analyze the impact of AI on human dignity in education and to outline the direction of its application based on the perspective of Catholic Social Teaching. A qualitative library research method was employed, utilizing content analysis and a critical-hermeneutic approach to examine documents from the Catholic Church's Magisterium and reputable scholarly journals. The findings indicate that the application of AI risks reducing learners to mere computational data and eroding their moral autonomy. The principles of human dignity (Imago Dei), the common good (bonum commune), subsidiarity, solidarity, and social justice prove relevant as an interpretive framework for positioning AI as an instrumental tool that serves integral human development.

items.title: Measuring risk preferences in large language models using adaptive binary search
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly support decision-making in high-stakes domains, where a model's risk preference, its tendency to favor lower-risk or higher-risk options under uncertainty, can shape the decisions it supports. Prior studies measuring these preferences in LLMs have produced mixed results. Several used fixed designs, such as choice lists, which locate the point where a preference changes only as finely as their preset values allow. Adaptive procedures, which adjust each query to earlier responses, concentrate measurement near that point and are established for eliciting human risk preferences. We present such a procedure for LLMs: it poses a choice between a lower-risk and a higher-risk option, varies the expected value of the higher-risk option across steps, locates by binary search the model's tipping point, the point at which its outputs shift to favor the higher-risk option, and reports it as an index of risk preference under one probability structure. We applied the procedure to eight LLMs from four providers (OpenAI, San Francisco, CA, USA; Anthropic, San Francisco, CA, USA; Google, Mountain View, CA, USA; xAI, Palo Alto, CA, USA), using emergency and disaster management vignettes, and tested whether presenting each option's expected value explicitly, rather than leaving it to be inferred, changed the measured preference. Median tipping points for six of the eight models fell near the point of equal expected value under both presentations. Claude Sonnet 4.6's tipping point was higher when the expected value was left to be inferred, with a shift whose bootstrap interval excludes 0; Claude Haiku 4.5's was higher as a point estimate, but its shift interval includes 0. In individual queries, deviations from expected-value maximization concentrated in four models: those of the two Anthropic models all toward the lower-risk option and those of the two Google models almost all toward the higher-risk option. Over the range queried in both presentations, presenting the expected value explicitly reduced these deviations in all four models. Because the two presentations convey the same expected values, the reduction indicates that these models did not respond to them as equivalent. The procedure applies to any model accessible via a text interface and is a reusable tool for comparing and screening models for risk-related decision support.

items.title: Navigating boundary-less work: how family-supportive leadership reshapes the impact of work-family blurring on professional women’s job engagement and taking charge in the digital transformation
items.abstract: In the context of a digital transformation that is fundamentally refining the nature of work and leadership dynamics, this research examines the mediating role of job engagement and the moderating role of family supportive supervisor behavior in the relationship between work-family role blurring and taking charge. A moderated mediation model is constructed using boundary theory and work-family border theory as foundational frameworks. The data were collected from 275 professional women in China. Moreover, family supportive supervisor behavior which is a key manifestation of supportive leadership in the modern, boundary-less workplace moderates the relationship between work-family role blurring and job engagement. Additionally, moderated mediation results confirm that a higher level of family supportive supervisor behavior increases professional women’s taking charge level through the indirect effect of work-family role blurring via job engagement. The findings highlight that in an era of pervasive digital connectivity, cultivating family supportive supervisor behaviors is a crucial strategy for management to mitigate role blurring and enhance professional women’s proactive workplace behaviors. This study enriches our understanding of the underlying processes of taking charge by developing a more comprehensive model that integrates the challenges of digital-era work design with the resource-providing function of leadership.

items.title: Off Service, with Purpose: Creating Learner-Centered Experiences for Off-Service Residents
items.abstract: Academic emergency departments (EDs) host off-service residents (OSRs) from various specialties. While OSRs contribute meaningfully to patient care, they often face unique challenges during their ED rotations, including limited preparation, heightened stress, and unmet personal expectations. Despite a standardized curriculum endorsed by the American College of Emergency Physicians, guidance on how to foster meaningful educational experiences for OSRs remains sparse. This perspective offers a structured approach grounded in self-determination theory (SDT), which emphasizes autonomy, competence, and relatedness as essential to intrinsic motivation and effective learning. By aligning educational strategies with SDT principles, emergency medicine educators can enhance engagement, support learner development, and create lasting interprofessional collaboration. Ultimately, this learner-centered approach not only enriches the OSR experience but also strengthens the role of the ED as a dynamic, inclusive learning environment for all trainees.

items.title: OPEN: A Benchmark Dataset and Baseline for Older Adult Patient Engagement Recognition in Virtual Rehabilitation Learning Environments
items.abstract: Engagement in virtual learning is critical to participant satisfaction, performance, and adherence, particularly in domains such as online education and virtual rehabilitation, where interactive communication is essential for success. However, accurately measuring engagement in virtual group settings remains a significant challenge. There is growing interest in leveraging artificial intelligence for large-scale, real-world, and automated engagement recognition. Although engagement has been widely studied among younger populations in academic contexts, research methods and datasets focused on older adults in virtual and telehealth learning environments remain limited. Existing approaches often overlook the contextual relevance of learning materials and the longitudinal dynamics of engagement across sessions. This paper presents OPEN (Older adult Patient ENgagement), a novel dataset created to support the development of artificial intelligence models for engagement recognition. The dataset was collected from eleven older adults participating in virtual group learning sessions over six weeks as part of their cardiac rehabilitation programs, yielding over 35 hours of data, which represents the largest dataset of its kind. While raw video is withheld to protect privacy, the publicly released data include facial, hand, and body joint landmarks, as well as behavioral and affective features extracted from video. Observational annotations comprise second-level binary engagement states, emotional and behavioral labels, and context-type details, such as whether the instructor addressed the group or an individual. Multiple versions of the dataset were generated using sample lengths of 5, 10, and 30 seconds, as well as variable-length segments. To demonstrate its utility, various machine learning and deep learning models were trained on the annotated data, achieving engagement recognition accuracy as high as 81%. OPEN provides a scalable foundation not only for advancing personalized, artificial intelligence-driven engagement recognition in aging populations but also for contributing to broader engagement recognition research.

items.title: Perceived AI literacy and TPACK in pre-service teacher education: mediating roles of perceived usefulness, ease of use, and value in blended learning
items.abstract: Background The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into blended learning requires pre-service teachers to develop AI-related competencies and the ability to integrate technology into pedagogy. This study examines how perceived AI literacy and technological pedagogical content knowledge (TPACK) are associated with deep learning through perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, and perceived value of AI use. Methods A cross-sectional survey was completed by 423 pre-service teachers enrolled in blended learning courses at a university in China. Data were analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM), with covariance-based structural equation modeling and fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis (fsQCA) used as complementary robustness and configurational analyses. Results Perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, and perceived value of AI use significantly mediated the relationships between the two competencies and deep learning. All six indirect pathways were significant in both the PLS-SEM and covariance-based SEM analyses. The fsQCA revealed an equifinal and asymmetric structure: multiple, partly substitutable conditions were sufficient for high deep learning, and no single condition was necessary for either high or low deep learning. Conclusions The findings integrate the technology acceptance model and expectancy-value theory to explain how pre-service teachers' competencies and perceptions relate to deep learning in AI-enhanced blended environments. Teacher education should support technical competence alongside positive perceptions of AI's utility, usability, and value. Because the measures were self-reported and collected cross-sectionally at one university, the findings are interpreted as associational and configurational rather than causal.

items.title: Perceptions of AI in veterinary medicine: insights from students, faculty, and practicing veterinarians in Hong Kong
items.abstract: Introduction As artificial intelligence (AI) transforms veterinary medicine, understanding stakeholder perceptions is crucial for its effective and responsible integration. To support the development of targeted educational and policy initiatives, this study aimed to evaluate the knowledge, attitudes, and practices regarding AI among Bachelor of Veterinary Medicine (BVM) students, PhD students, faculty, and practicing veterinarians in Hong Kong. Methods A cross-sectional online survey was conducted between December 2023 and March 2024 among BVM students, PhD students, and faculty members at City University of Hong Kong, and practicing veterinarians in Hong Kong who are members of the Hong Kong Veterinary Association. The survey assessed participants’ familiarity with AI, prior training, perceived benefits, concerns, and willingness to adopt AI in education and clinical practice. Descriptive and comparative analyses were performed to examine differences across stakeholder groups. Results Of 79 complete responses, nearly half (46.8%) reported unfamiliarity with AI concepts. Only 17.7% had received formal AI training, although 78.5% expressed interest in future AI education. Most respondents agreed that AI could enhance veterinary teaching and practice (83.5%) and 81.0% indicated they would likely incorporate AI tools into their work. Key perceived benefits included support for case-based learning (83.5%), virtual animal models for teaching (77.2%), and improved diagnostic accuracy (74.7%). However, 41.8% felt inadequately prepared to use AI. Major concerns included veterinarian accountability for AI-related harms (79.7%), lack of system flexibility (75.9%), and potential clinical inaccuracies (70.9%). Descriptively, practicing veterinarians reported the lowest AI tool use (66.7% had never used AI tools), the lowest preparedness (66.7% felt unprepared), and lower agreement with AI’s clinical benefits, although attitude differences were not statistically significant. Conclusion These exploratory findings suggest gaps in self-reported AI knowledge and differing perceptions of AI across veterinary stakeholder groups in Hong Kong, with AI use already widespread at the time of the survey despite limited formal training. While enthusiasm for AI integration is high, concerns about preparedness, accuracy, and ethical responsibility remain. Larger, multi-institutional studies are needed to confirm these patterns and to inform targeted training programs and ethical frameworks for safe and effective AI adoption in veterinary medicine.

items.title: Predicting Motion Sickness Sensitivity
items.abstract: Objective To determine the combined effectiveness of personal factors in predicting motion sickness sensitivity elicited by linear motion of a sled. Background Technologies that create challenging motion environments have spurred the development of mathematical models aimed at predicting motion sickness. Including personal factors may improve their predictive accuracy. History of motion sickness, age, gender, and visual dependence have been identified as potential predictors, although their individual predictive value is limited. Method We assessed motion sickness history, age, and gender through a questionnaire. To evaluate visual dependence, participants oriented a virtual rod parallel to the orientation of gravity while observing a tilted static frame or a disc rotating in roll. Sensitivity is expressed using a new measure that considers both the magnitude and accumulation of self-reported symptoms. Results Our results confirmed the predictive value of history and showed a small yet significant contribution of dynamic visual dependence, with greater dependence associated with higher sensitivity ( R 2 = 25%). Recent history reported over the past 10 years was demonstrated as a better predictor than lifetime history. Age, gender, and static visual dependence did not enhance the prediction. Conclusion Combining multiple predictors shows little advantage for improving a prediction of sensitivity beyond history alone. Future studies could confirm the predictive value of dynamic visual dependence and seek to optimize recent history, for example, by restricting time period and motion environment. Application Improved prediction models may support tailoring system parameters to user sensitivity in technologies such as automated driving, head mounted displays, and simulators.

items.title: Professional choice motivation and flow experience in specialized skill courses: a three-way interaction analysis among undergraduate physical education majors
items.abstract: Specialized skill courses are a crucial component of talent cultivation in physical education programs. However, their long duration and high intensity often lead to declines in student engagement, thereby affecting skill acquisition. Flow experience, as a key psychological indicator of learning states, can effectively reflect students’ actual level of involvement. Focusing on professional choice motivation, this study examined its relationship with flow experience in specialized skill courses among undergraduate physical education majors and further tested the three-way interaction among professional choice motivation, physical self-efficacy, and physical activity volume. Using the Professional Choice Motivation Scale, Physical Self-Efficacy Scale, Physical Activity Rating Scale, and the absorption subscale of the Flow Short Scale, data were collected on two survey occasions 3 months apart. A total of 398 valid responses were obtained at T1, and 203 valid responses were obtained when the T1 participants were surveyed again at T2. Because individual responses could not be matched across the two occasions, the two datasets were analyzed separately. Pearson correlation analysis, multiple linear regression, three-way interaction analysis, and conditional effect tests were performed using R. The results showed that both intrinsic motivation ( β T1 = 0.72, β T2 = 0.64, p T1T2 < 0.001) and extrinsic motivation ( β T1 = 0.61, β T2 = 0.53, p T1T2 < 0.001) were significantly and positively associated with flow experience at both survey occasions. Furthermore, the three-way interaction among professional choice motivation, physical self-efficacy, and physical activity volume was significant at both T1 and T2 and showed the same negative direction ( p T1T2 < 0.05). Conditional effect tests showed that, except for the high physical activity volume/high physical self-efficacy condition at T2, intrinsic motivation and extrinsic motivation were significantly and positively associated with flow experience under all other conditions. These findings contribute to a more contextualized understanding of the relationship between professional choice motivation and flow experience and offer important theoretical implications for instructional practice in specialized skill courses.

items.title: Prompting Metacognition: Using Prompt Writing as a Language Task and Metacognitive Tool in ELT
items.abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) tools have made their way into English Language Teaching (ELT) contexts, yet their pedagogical value remains contested. While many learners engage with GenAI primarily as a quick hack for producing answers, fewer use it as a resource for reflective language learning. This study explores prompt writing as a language learning task that supports both language development and metacognitive awareness. The study was conducted with a target group of pre-seminary, tertiary-level learners with mixed linguistic proficiency. Over the course of four instructional sessions, the study used a classroom-based action research design. Learners engaged in cycles of prompt drafting, GenAI-generated responses, peer discussion, and prompt refinement. Classroom observations, learner reflections, and group discussions were used to gather qualitative insights. The findings indicate measurable improvement in learners’ autonomy, as learners became aware of how lexical choices shape meaning, along with increased engagement, teamwork, and reflective thinking. The study argues that prompt writing, when treated as a language task rather than a technical skill, can function as a practical tool for fostering metacognition in ELT classrooms.

items.title: Psychosocial Working Conditions in a Portuguese Social Care Institution: A Descriptive Case Study by Occupational Group
items.abstract: Abstract: Psychosocial working conditions have become an increasingly relevant concern in occupational health, particularly in social care contexts where employees are exposed to demanding emotional and physical environments. This study examines the main psychosocial factors affecting workers in a Portuguese private social solidarity institution and explores their implications for well-being and productivity. A descriptive quantitative case study was conducted, supported by a literature review and a questionnaire applied to different professional groups within the organisation. The findings suggest that, although overall levels of psychosocial risk are relatively low, there are meaningful differences across occupational categories. Frontline care workers appear to be the most exposed group, followed by kitchen staff and technical personnel. Across the sample, emotional and physical demands, work pace, task overload and limited recognition emerged as the most significant factors. These results indicate that even in seemingly stable organisational environments, certain roles remain particularly vulnerable to psychosocial strain. The study underscores the importance of adopting preventive and organisational measures to foster healthier, more supportive working conditions, as these are essential for both employee well-being and the quality of care provided. Keywords: psychosocial risks, mental health, charitable organisations, working conditions, well-being at work. ___________________ Condições Psicossociais de Trabalho numa Instituição Portuguesa de Apoio Social: Um Estudo de Caso Descritivo por Grupo Profissional Resumo: As condições de trabalho psicossociais têm-se tornado uma preocupação cada vez mais relevante na saúde ocupacional, particularmente em contextos de assistência social, onde os trabalhadores estão expostos a ambientes emocional e fisicamente exigentes. Este estudo analisa os principais fatores psicossociais que afetam os trabalhadores de uma instituição privada de solidariedade social portuguesa e explora as suas implicações para o bem-estar e a produtividade. Foi realizado um estudo de caso quantitativo descritivo, apoiado por uma revisão da literatura e por um questionário aplicado a diferentes grupos profissionais dentro da organização. Os resultados sugerem que, embora os níveis globais de risco psicossocial sejam relativamente baixos, existem diferenças significativas entre as categorias profissionais. Os profissionais de cuidados na linha da frente parecem ser o grupo mais exposto, seguidos pelo pessoal de cozinha e pelo pessoal técnico. Em toda a amostra, as exigências emocionais e físicas, o ritmo de trabalho, a sobrecarga de tarefas e o reconhecimento limitado emergiram como os fatores mais significativos. Estes resultados indicam que, mesmo em ambientes organizacionais aparentemente estáveis, certas funções permanecem particularmente vulneráveis à tensão psicossocial. items.title: Reconstructing Core Competencies of Front-Office Employees in South Korean Professional Sports Organizations in the Era of Artificial Intelligence: A Delphi Study
items.abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly reshapes organizational decision-making, fan engagement, and business operations, the competencies expected of front-office employees are also evolving. This study aimed to reconstruct the core competencies required of front-office employees in South Korean professional sports organizations in the AI era. To this end, a three-round Delphi study was conducted with 20 experts from academia, South Korean professional sports organizations, and research institutes. The Delphi process involved generating competency items, evaluating their relevance, and establishing expert consensus regarding the final competency framework. The findings identified 28 competency items grouped into the following five competency domains: Data & AI Utilization Competency, Human–AI Collaboration Competency, Marketing & Fan Engagement Competency, Communication & Execution Competency, and Ethics & Values Competency. These findings suggest that competencies in AI-enabled professional sports organizations extend beyond technical proficiency and warrant an integrated combination of technological, collaborative, organizational, relational, and ethical capabilities. This study refines the application of competency theory to AI-supported work by providing a context-specific framework for front-office employees in South Korean professional sports organizations. The proposed framework offers a foundation for understanding how South Korean professional sports organizations may reconstruct workforce competencies in response to the evolving demands of the AI era.

items.title: REPOSITIONING NIGERIAN POLYTECHNIC CHEMISTRY PROGRAMMES FOR THE FOURTH INDUSTRIAL REVOLUTION: A CONCEPTUAL FRAMEWORK FOR EMBEDDING ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN THE CURRICULUM
items.abstract: The emergence of the Fourth Industrial Revolution (Industry 4.0) is fundamentally altering the landscape of the global chemical sector through automation, cyber-physical infrastructures, machine learning, and data-intensive approaches to discovery. These shifts have generated an acute need for professionals who can function effectively at the convergence of chemistry, computation, and digital technologies. In contrast, Nigerian polytechnics (institutions constitutionally tasked with cultivating mid-level technical expertise) continue to operate largely conventional, content-saturated chemistry curricula that show little correspondence with these evolving workforce expectations. This conceptual study set out to examine how artificial intelligence (AI) could be systematically woven into the chemistry curricula of Nigerian polytechnics as a means of equipping graduates for Industry 4.0. By triangulating scholarship on AI in education, chemistry pedagogy, technical and vocational education and training (TVET), and Industry 4.0 workforce requirements, the paper constructed a conceptual architecture for curriculum integration and evaluated four distinct integration pathways: the supplementary, embedded, dual-track, and fully reformed models. The analysis also interrogated the structural, human-capital, infrastructural, ethical, and policy-related obstacles that impede AI uptake within Nigerian polytechnics, while delineating the Industry 4.0 capabilities that chemistry graduates must command—namely data literacy, computational reasoning, digitally mediated laboratory competence, and AI-supported problem resolution. The study concludes that a staged, context-attuned integration approach—anchored in purposeful policy reform, lecturer capacity building, industry collaboration, and deliberate investment in digital infrastructure—is indispensable for sustaining the relevance of Nigerian polytechnics. Concrete recommendations are advanced for curriculum authorities, institutional managers, and industry stakeholders.

items.title: Revisiting Starr (1969)—Social Benefit Versus Technological Risk: What is Our Society Willing to Pay for Safety?
items.abstract: Abstract This contribution examines how societies perceive and manage technological risks, focusing on the ethical and economic dimensions of valuing human life. Technological advancements have historically improved quality of life but have introduced risks requiring trade-offs between safety and cost. Starr’s seminal 1969 study, later corroborated by further research, illustrated that voluntary risks are tolerated at much higher levels than involuntary ones, and that public acceptance of risk depends on perceived benefits. Since Starr’s publication, the popularity of cost-benefit analysis in decision-making has increased exponentially, yet it still struggles to capture key ethical, social, and psychological factors, making purely rational models insufficient. Today, the unanticipated increase in data availability and the development of processing infrastructure might provide opportunities. However, emerging technologies such as artificial intelligence introduce new forms of risk that require careful consideration and open debate. Ultimately, what our society is willing to pay for safety can only be answered through inclusive and adaptive risk governance approaches with safeguards against power imbalance and tunnel vision, fostering public trust and transparent deliberation of values and ethical dilemmas rather than relying solely on numeric thresholds or precedents.

items.title: Should there be a teacher in-the-loop? A study of generative AI-personalized tasks middle school
items.abstract: Abstract Large language models can be used to design instructional tasks to align to students’ needs. These generative AI models can create tasks that correspond to students’ out-of-school interests in areas like sports or music, which may enhance students’ interest in learning. However, little is known about teachers’ processes for creating or modifying tasks with generative AI, despite commercial AI companies’ claims that they will save teachers time. In the present study, 7 middle school mathematics teachers used ChatGPT to create personalized versions of problems in their curriculum to correspond to their students’ interests. The prompting moves teachers made and their students’ open-ended feedback on personalized problems were examined through thematic analysis. Teachers’ efficiency when creating problems and the ratings of their 7th grade students who received personalized assignments were examined. Results from this sample suggest that having a teacher-in-the-loop may result in generative AI-enhanced personalization being enacted at a broad grain size, whereas students often expressed preference for a smaller grain-size where they receive specific popular culture references that interest them. Teachers used prompting to adjust popular culture references and address issues with the depth, ethics, or realism of the problems generated, in some cases showing epistemic agency. The article closes with an exploratory, design-focused look at scalability trade-offs with teacher-facing personalization, patterns of teacher prompting practices, and opportunities for teachers to exercise epistemic and ethical monitoring of personalization outputs.

items.abstract: This paper is part of an independent five-part research series on institutional governance, administrative gatekeeping, and frontline operational practice: Part I: Skynet and HAL 9000: From Science Fiction to Systems Engineering (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23534494) Part II: Commercial Metrics vs. Epistemic Rigour (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23567195) Part III: Automated Confirmation Bias (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23615567) Part IV: Beyond Institutional Risk (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23615568) Part V: Sycophancy as an Asset in LLM Technology (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23886622.) This paper establishes a foundational inversion in how Large Language Models (LLMs) alter the balance of power between entrenched institutions and individual practitioners. While closed institutional deployments of LLMs risk generating automated confirmation bias and epistemic laundering, the intrinsic trait of model sycophancy—long viewed by safety engineers as a severe design defect—functions as a vital asset when harnessed for individual advocacy. By making every effort to support the user's case against the odds, an LLM provides unshakeable psychological safety, non-judgmental iteration, and immediate register translation. Drawing on historical case studies across clinical nursing and skilled manual trades at institutions like Hawker Siddeley, this paper demonstrates how frontline workers can leverage model sycophancy to strip the managerial elite of their linguistic monopoly, bypass credentialist gatekeeping, and project an unyielding, authoritative voice against administrative power. Furthermore, this manuscript is intentionally submitted into formal channels as a methodological Trojan horse—using the structural forms of academic and professional publishing to subvert institutional gatekeeping from within. Keywords: LLM Sycophancy, Institutional Gatekeeping, Frontline Agency, Technical Imperialism, Operational Translation, Systems Safety Engineering, Information Management

items.title: Task-Specific Impacts of Cognitive Fatigue on Subjective Experience and Psychomotor Performance
items.abstract: Objective To determine how cognitive fatigue (CF) affects subjective experience and reaction time (RT) performance across tasks with different processing demands (simple, go/no-go, choice), and whether these effects depend on the type of fatigue-inducing mental work. Background CF is a psychobiological state of subjective exhaustion from mental effort that can compromise workplace productivity and safety. Although slowed RT is an often-observed consequence of CF, it is unclear how this compares across RT paradigms and fatigue-inducing tasks. Method Using a remotely administered experiment, 402 participants completed a 60-minute CF (Math-Memory, Stroop, Time Load Dual-Back) or control (documentary) intervention. Subjective ratings (mental fatigue, motivation) and RT performance (simple, go/no-go, choice) were assessed pre- and post-intervention. Results Relative to control, all CF tasks increased subjective fatigue ( p < .001), while motivation declined following Dual-Back and Stroop ( p ≤ .030) but not Math-Memory. Simple and choice RT slowed significantly following all CF interventions vs control ( p < .010), with the greatest choice RT slowing after Stroop ( p ≤ .032). Only Stroop produced significant go/no-go RT slowing ( p = .004). Conclusion Subjective fatigue and simple RT were broadly sensitive to CF, indicating general psychomotor slowing. Conversely, motivation and higher-complexity RT measures showed task-specific effects, perhaps reflecting overlap between fatigue-inducing and RT task demands. Application Task type is important when considering RT as a fatigue assessment tool. These findings support multidimensional (subjective and RT) CF assessments and indicate that simple RT may be effective for rapid, broad fatigue monitoring, whereas complex RT metrics may be useful when exploring task-specific executive processing effects.

items.title: Teachers’ attitudes and behavioural intentions towards AI integration in Chinese higher education: a qualitative interview study
items.abstract: Introduction The rapid expansion of generative AI has intensified scholarly and policy debate over its role in higher education, yet university teachers’ attitudes towards its integration remain complex and context-dependent. This study explores how university teachers perceive, experience, and respond to AI integration in their teaching. Guided primarily by the three-component attitude model and informed by the technology acceptance model and the theory of planned behaviour, the study examines cognitive appraisals, affective responses, behavioural intentions, and perceived support needs. Methods The study draws on semi-structured interviews with 14 university teachers from four higher education institutions in China. The interview data were analysed using codebook-informed thematic analysis combining deductive and inductive coding. Results The findings indicate that teachers generally perceive AI as a supportive rather than substitutive educational tool, valuing it for improving efficiency, supporting lesson preparation, and enriching pedagogical design. Emotional responses varied from enthusiasm and a sense of accomplishment to caution, neutrality, and, in some cases, declining satisfaction. Across the interviews, teachers’ primary concerns centred less on their own replacement than on the perceived risks of inappropriate AI use for students’ independent thinking, reasoning, originality, and authentic understanding. Teachers’ intentions to adopt AI were therefore conditional and bounded, shaped by pedagogical purpose, disciplinary context, student readiness, and the need to maintain teacher control. Teachers also emphasised that sustainable AI integration requires more than general encouragement, calling instead for AI literacy development, discipline-sensitive support, specialised tools, and enabling institutional infrastructure. Discussion Overall, these findings extend contextual understandings of teachers’ AI acceptance by showing how adoption intentions are pedagogically negotiated and highlight the importance of supporting professional judgement and students’ independent thinking in higher education.

items.title: Teachers’ basic psychological need satisfactions and their intentions to use generative artificial intelligence: the mediating role of engagement in professional development
items.abstract: Introduction Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) offers new opportunities for instructional innovation, yet the psychological mechanisms underlying teachers’ intentions to adopt it remain unclear. Intrinsic motivation is an important internal factor shaping teachers’ intentions to use GenAI and is closely linked to the satisfaction of their basic psychological needs. Drawing on self-determination theory (SDT), this study develops and tests a theoretical framework linking teachers’ basic psychological need satisfaction to their intention to use GenAI through intrinsic motivation and engagement in professional development. Such engagement may foster innovation in GenAI-supported teaching practices. Methods Survey data were collected from 146 teachers participating in a GenAI learning program. Structural equation modeling was used to examine the hypothesized relationships among basic psychological need satisfaction, intrinsic motivation, engagement in professional development, and intention to use GenAI. Results Perceived competence in using GenAI was significantly and positively associated with intrinsic motivation, whereas perceived autonomy and relatedness were not significantly associated with intrinsic motivation. Engagement in professional development mediated the relationship between intrinsic motivation and intention to use GenAI. Discussion These findings provide a nuanced understanding of the psychological mechanisms underlying teachers’ intentions to adopt GenAI, highlighting the roles of perceived competence, intrinsic motivation, and engagement in professional development. They also offer practical implications for supporting the integration of GenAI into teaching.

items.title: The Effect of AI Absorptive Capacity of Organizations on Workers’ Perceptions About Smart Work Environment Perception Towards Digital Innovation Behavior.
items.abstract: This study investigates the effect of organizational artificial intelligence (AI) absorptive capacity on employees’ perceptions of the smart work environment and how these perceptions influence their digital innovative behavior in the telecommunications industry, with Digital Transformational Leadership as a moderating variable. In this study, two important theoretical perspectives were utilized: Absorptive Capacity Theory, which highlights how organizations acquire, assimilate, and apply their knowledge related to AI, and Socio-Technical Systems Theory, which addresses the connection between technology and the social aspect of the working environment. A quantitative research design was used through partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM). The data were gathered from 279 respondents working in the telecommunication industry in Jordan. These respondents worked for internet service providers, network operators, and mobile network operators. The findings show that organizational AI absorptive capacity has a strong positive effect on Smart Work Environment Perception (β = 0.742), which in turn enhances Digital Innovative Behavior (β = 0.681). Smart Work Environment Perception partially mediates the relationship between AI absorptive capacity and Digital Innovative Behavior (indirect effect β = 0.506), while Digital Transformational Leadership positively moderates the relationship between AI absorptive capacity and the smart work environment (β = 0.276) and between the smart work environment and Digital Innovative Behavior (β = 0.241). The current research adds value to the literature surrounding AI adoption within organizations by examining how technical capabilities and organizational leadership help foster Digital Innovative Behavior in the telecommunications industry.

items.title: The Effect of Generative AI and Gamification on Enhancing Students’ Motivation Based on the ARCS Model
items.abstract: High school biology learning is often hindered by abstract concepts and cognitive overload, leading to low student motivation. Although generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) and gamification show instructional potential, their combined motivational effects remain underexplored. Grounded in the ARCS model, this study examined the impact of integrating ChatGPT-based GenAI and gamification on students’ Attention, Relevance, Confidence, and Satisfaction. A longitudinal quasi-experimental repeated measures design was conducted with 52 high school biology students over eight weeks. Motivation was measured at four time points using a validated ARCS questionnaire and analyzed with Wilcoxon signed-rank tests. Results showed significant improvements across all ARCS dimensions from pre- to post-intervention (p < .001). Attention and relevance increased steadily, confidence improved in later stages, and satisfaction rose overall. Reported challenges included limited personalized AI feedback, competition-induced anxiety associated with leaderboard-based competition, and increased cognitive load resulting from complex AI-generated content. The findings indicate that GenAI-supported gamification can enhance motivation in biology learning when supported by careful pedagogical design.

items.title: The Effects of Corporate AI Environment Factors on Employees’ Technology Acceptance Attitude and Continuous Intention to Use
items.abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes an imperative survival strategy for modern enterprises, numerous organizations continue to face implementation failures stemming from employees’ psychological resistance. To address the scarcity of empirical research regarding the practical and psychological acceptance of AI in workflows, this study investigates the structural relationships between technological maturity and users’ cognitive adoption. Grounded in an integrated framework utilizing the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), this research conceptualizes the “AI Environment Factor” as a higher-order construct comprising four foundational sub-dimensions: AI System Quality, AI Information Quality, AI Data Quality, and AI Infrastructure. A quantitative survey was administered to 189 corporate practitioners who have utilized enterprise-wide AI systems for at least one year, and the empirical data were analyzed using Structural Equation Modeling (SEM). The analytical results indicate that the AI Environment Factor exerts a statistically significant positive effect on both Perceived Ease of Use and Perceived Usefulness. Furthermore, Perceived Ease of Use was found to positively influence Perceived Usefulness. Ultimately, both Perceived Ease of Use and Perceived Usefulness are significantly associated with the employees’ continuous AI Intention to Use. These findings theoretically contribute to the literature by providing a measurable structural model for the continuance intention phase of organizational AI adoption. Practically, this study offers actionable guidelines for corporate executives, emphasizing that securing rigorous data accuracy and a stable system infrastructure is indispensable for mitigating cognitive load, fostering innovative corporate cultures, and maximizing the efficacy of AI utilization.

items.title: The Influence of Employees' Integration of Generative Artificial Intelligence Tools on Organizational Data Exposure Risks Within the Context of Data Security Posture in Uganda
items.abstract: The rapid diffusion of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) tools such as ChatGPT, Gemini, Copilot, and Claude into everyday work practices has created a new and poorly governed channel through which organizational data can leave the enterprise. This review synthesized theoretical, empirical, and practitioner literature on the relationship between employees' integration of GenAI tools and organizational data exposure risks, situating that relationship within the broader context of organizational data security posture. The review is organized around four themes, the extent, drivers, and patterns of employee GenAI integration in the workplace, the phenomenon of "Shadow AI" and "Bring Your Own AI" (BYOAI), the mechanisms through which GenAI use generates data exposure, leakage, and compliance risks, and the role of data security posture encompassing governance frameworks, visibility, policy, and employee security behavior in moderating those risks. Literature from developed economies dominates the field, while evidence from Uganda and the wider Sub-Saharan African context remains scarce. The review identifies key theoretical anchors (the Technology Acceptance Model, Protection Motivation Theory, and information security governance perspectives), synthesized documented incidents such as the Samsung ChatGPT data leak, and highlights empirical survey evidence showing widespread unsanctioned use of GenAI by employees. It concludes by delineating conceptual and empirical gaps particularly the absence of studies that jointly model GenAI integration, data exposure risk, and data security posture in developing country organizational settings and proposes a conceptual framework to guide future research in Ugandan organizations.

items.title: The mediating role of self-efficacy in the relationships of technophilia and positive emotional experience with perceived learning effectiveness in AI-supported EFL education
items.abstract: Abstract Despite the increasing integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into English as a Foreign Language (EFL) education, the psychological mechanisms linking learners’ technological dispositions and emotional experiences to perceived learning effectiveness remain undertheorized and empirically underexplored. This study examined whether self-efficacy served as a statistical mediator in the relationships of technophilia and positive emotional experience with perceived learning effectiveness in AI-supported EFL education. A cross-sectional survey was conducted involving 234 students enrolled in English-language courses at a private college of health sciences. Adapted multi-item scales on technophilia, positive emotional experience, self-efficacy, and perceived learning effectiveness were administered. Structural equation modeling with bootstrapping (5000 resamples) was used to examine direct and indirect associations. Self-efficacy demonstrated the strongest direct association with perceived learning effectiveness (β = 0.375, p = 0.001). Positive emotional experience was strongly associated with self-efficacy (β = 0.624, p < 0.001), and its indirect association with perceived learning effectiveness through self-efficacy was significant (β = 0.234, 95% CI [0.128, 0.351]). Technophilia was also positively associated with self-efficacy (β = 0.307, p = 0.002), and its indirect association with perceived learning effectiveness through self-efficacy was significant. The findings were consistent with self-efficacy partially mediating both relationships. These findings suggest that learners’ confidence in managing AI-supported tasks plays an important role in linking affective dispositions to perceived effectiveness appraisals. The study contributes to computer-assisted language learning (CALL) research by clarifying how positive orientation toward AI-supported technologies, emotional experience, and efficacy beliefs jointly relate to learners’ perceptions of effective AI-supported language learning. Pedagogically, the findings suggest that progressively scaffolded practice and mastery-oriented AI tasks may strengthen self-efficacy and improve learners’ perceived effectiveness in AI-supported EFL environments.

items.title: The Paradox of Algorithmic Sycophancy: Sycophancy in Large Language Models and the Limits of AI-Mediated Knowledge Reconstruction in the Metacognitive Creative Destruction Model
items.abstract: The Metacognitive Creative Destruction (MCD) model approaches educational innovation as a perpetual spiral process. Contradiction (accumulated cognitive conflicts that resist interpretation), activates Metacognitive Capacity, enabling Destructive Unlearning Propensity, the conscious abandonment of outdated mental schemas, which in turn enables Creative Reconstruction Ability, and ultimately, new knowledge. In the model’s empirical validation with 1,498 teachers, a critical finding emerged: AI Augmentation Intensity (AIA) predicted Metacognitive Capacity (MC) and Creative Reconstruction Ability (CRA), but not Destructive Unlearning Propensity (DUP).This article argues that this finding is not accidental, but reflects an inherent weakness of modern AI systems, and more specifically, the tendency toward AI Sycophancy. Models trained with reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) tend to avoid disagreements and be likable to the user, preventing the individual from experiencing cognitive conflicts, perpetuating their already formed beliefs at the expense of scientific accuracy.Therefore, in an environment of “algorithmic flattery”, the necessary contradictions that trigger unlearning are not produced. Based on the MCD model, it is concluded that the absence of unlearning, that is, the deliberate and conscious abandonment of outdated beliefs, mental models and practices, makes the reconstruction of knowledge absolutely superficial and thus, algorithmically condescending interaction does not produce deep and authentic knowledge, regardless of AI Augmentation Intensity.

items.abstract: Most biographies follow a life through time. This one follows a life through an equation. Satish Gajawada, an Integrated Dual Degree (B.Tech + M.Tech) graduate of the Indian Institute of Technology Roorkee (2012), has spent fourteen years as an independent researcher who gives names, structure and heart to ideas in artificial intelligence: Excellent AI (EAI), Very Highly Advanced AI (VHAAI), Out of the Box AI (OBAI), a society (ISVHAAI), a family of value-themed swarm algorithms, thirteen theories of human purpose, a 108-right taxonomy of human rights, and a lifelong “thesis” supervised by his parents and GOD. Reading the particle swarm update rule as a metaphor for a research life, this article identifies four forces (inertia, personal best, global best and exploration) and one outcome: a position update that, in 2026, turned decisively toward testing and open disclosure. Drawing on eight source documents, with each statement attributed to a published work, a manuscript or the subject’s own account, we show that a reproducible genetic-algorithm and PSO experiment found a fairness weight that cut a demographic-parity gap from 0.121 to 0.016 for 1.9 points of accuracy, and a gentler weight that improved accuracy and fairness together. Itemised output rose from one entry in 2012 to twelve in 2026. We conclude that Gajawada is a builder of human-centred vocabulary and institutions, a grateful son, a joyful experimenter and a candid author, and that his life offers every learner a portable update rule: keep your direction, honour your best, listen to your guides, stay curious, and keep moving.

items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly influencing Englishlanguage learning by providing personalized instruction, immediate feedback,interactive communication, and opportunities for independent practice. This paperexamines the potential benefits and challenges of integrating AI technologies intoEnglish as a Foreign Language (EFL) learning. The study adopts a literature reviewapproach and draws on existing empirical research, systematic reviews, andinternational educational guidance. The reviewed literature suggests that AI-supportedlearning can contribute to language development, particularly by providing writingfeedback, facilitating conversational practice, and supporting learner engagement.However, the effectiveness of these technologies depends on the quality of AIgenerated feedback, learners’ digital literacy, appropriate pedagogical guidance, andresponsible use. Potential challenges include inaccurate information, excessivedependence on AI, academic integrity concerns, and data privacy risks. The paperargues that AI should complement rather than replace teachers and meaningful humaninteraction. It concludes that the responsible integration of AI into English languageeducation requires clear learning objectives, critical evaluation of AI-generated content,and a balanced combination of technological tools and teacher-led instruction.

items.title: The role of social media and generative-ai in self-directed learning among respiratory therapy interns: a qualitative study
items.abstract: Social media and generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) are increasingly integrated into healthcare education and have the potential to enhance self-directed learning (SDL). Although these technologies are widely used by healthcare students, little is known about how respiratory therapy interns use social media and GenAI to support their SDL during clinical training. This qualitative study adopted an interpretivist approach to explore respiratory therapy interns’ experiences of using social media and generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) to support self-directed learning (SDL). A total population sampling strategy was employed, whereby all 25 eligible respiratory therapy interns undertaking their internship at one Saudi hospital were invited to participate. Nineteen interns consented to participate and completed semi-structured interviews. Data were analyzed using Braun and Clarke’s thematic analysis. Four themes were identified. First, participants conceptualized SDL as an independent learning process in which they assumed responsibility for identifying learning needs and seeking knowledge using digital resources. Second, social media supported SDL by providing accessible educational content, facilitating peer learning and collaboration, identifying learning needs, and supporting examination preparation. Third, GenAI functioned as a personalized learning assistant by simplifying complex concepts, summarizing learning materials and generating practice questions. Finally, participants stressed the importance of responsible use of digital technologies by critically evaluating information, verifying content using trusted sources and recognizing challenges including misinformation, distraction, plagiarism concerns and overreliance on GenAI. Respiratory therapy interns have integrated social media and GenAI into their self-directed learning in both academic and clinical contexts. These technologies complement rather than replace traditional learning resources and may enhance learner autonomy when used critically and responsibly. Healthcare education programs should enable students to develop AI literacy and self-directed learning skills to optimize the educational benefits of emerging technologies while promoting effective use.

items.title: The Website as Brand Source of Truth: Grounding AI-Generated Marketing Content in What a Company Already Says
items.abstract: Generative AI can write scripts, captions and scenes for a company in seconds, but when it is prompted from scratch it fills gaps with plausible inventions and drifts away from what the company actually says about itself. This paper argues that a company's own website is the natural source of truth for AI-generated marketing, provided it is turned into a structured brand record that a person reviews before use. We review evidence that brand equity rests on coherent brand knowledge and that a brand's website shapes how the brand is perceived; that language models hallucinate for documented reasons and drift from their instructions over a conversation; and that grounding generation in retrieved sources reduces hallucination without removing it. Models also tend to follow the context they are given, even when it is wrong, and web content can be outdated or carry injected instructions. From this evidence we derive six design principles, among them reading what the company already publishes, keeping human edits authoritative over automatic re-reads, separating what was read from what was invented, and treating web content as data rather than instructions. We illustrate the principles with GetReelCom, which drafts a reviewable brand record from a company's website, described from its public documentation, and we propose an evaluation. Competing interests: the author is a co-founder of GetReelCom, the application used as the illustrative case. About the author: Amber Kesselaer is a growth consultant and an expert in marketing and AI video generation.

items.title: Theory-Guided Human-AI Collaboration: Focusing, Feedback and Critical Examination in Jean-Pol Martin's Semantic Field
items.abstract: This methodological article examines how Jean-Pol Martin organizes theory-guided collaboration with artificial intelligence through two complementary documents: a theory prompt and a master prompt. The theory prompt supplies the conceptual framework of Learning by Teaching (LdL), the New Human Rights (NMR), and Martin’s semantic field. The master prompt specifies analytical procedures, working expectations, and criteria for provisional claims. Ongoing human feedback connects these instructions to the concrete task. The article’s contribution lies in making the relationship between conceptual grounding, procedural direction, and situated correction explicit. Two episodes from the dialogue leading to this publication illustrate how editorial feedback and the introduction of foundational documents reshape an AI-generated text. Within the developing series on LdL, NMR, and human-AI collaboration, the article functions as a methodological bridge between theoretical exposition and practical application. It offers a reusable procedure for documenting instructions, corrections, and revisions, together with suggestions for comparative evaluation. The organismic reference point of the NMR framework places the living, thinking, social, and meaning-oriented human being at the centre of analysis. Six equal-ranking needs provide its anthropological and normative orientation: thinking, health, security, social belonging, self-realization and participation, and meaning. This is a methodological account with illustrative dialogue episodes, not a controlled study. It distinguishes conceptual coherence from factual validation and practical effectiveness. The article was developed through collaboration between Jean-Pol Martin and ChatGPT. Supplementary materials: The deposit includes the original German master prompt and theory prompt with its organismic supplement. The main article is in English; the supplementary documents are in German.

items.title: TRANSHUMANISM IN THE AGE OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE:THE SOCIO-PHILOSOPHICAL DIMENSIONS OF THE DIGITAL SOCIETY
items.abstract: The relevance of the study. The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence, biotechnology, and neural interfaces underscores the need for a socio-philosophical analysis of transhumanism as a philosophical movement that advocates the possibility and desirability of technologically enhancing human nature. As digital society takes shape, transhumanist ideas are moving beyond academic discourse to become a driving force behind real-world social transformations, raising fundamentally new questions about the nature of human agency, the boundaries between the natural and the artificial, and the future social order. This article aims to examine the socio-philosophical dimensions of transhumanism in the age of artificial intelligence through an analysis of the movement’s key conceptual foundations, its interconnection with the processes of digitalisation, and a critical reflection on the associated risks and prospects. The study’s methodological framework is based on its stated aim and research objectives and adopts an interdisciplinary approach drawing on social philosophy, technology ethics, the social sciences, and media studies. The study employs comparative- historical analysis, the phenomenological method, critical discourse analysis, and a systems approach to investigating the social consequences of technological development. Research findings. The intellectual origins of transhumanism have been traced, from FM-2030’s futurist manifestos to contemporary concepts of the technological singularity and superintelligence. The analysis shows that digital society creates a distinct socio-technical environment in which transhumanist transformations assume concrete forms and give rise to new social tensions. Three key tensions within the transhumanist project have been identified: between individual freedom of self-improvement and its systemic social consequences; between techno-optimistic predictions and the real risks of humanity losing control over powerful technological systems; and between the pursuit of boundless self-improvement and the threat posed by the erosion of essential human qualities as the foundation of moral and legal equality. It is emphasised that a socio-philosophical understanding of transhumanism requires moving beyond the binary opposition between techno-optimism and technophobia in favour of a balanced, critical, and humanistically oriented approach that combines recognition of the genuine possibilities of technological progress with responsible consideration of its limits and risks.

items.title: Trust in artificial intelligence and AI-assisted social and civic decision-making among Arab youth: evidence from Egypt, Kuwait, and the UAE
items.abstract: Introduction Trust in artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly shapes how young people evaluate information and public issues, yet evidence from Arab contexts remains limited. This study examined the socio-technical correlates of trust in AI and its association with AI-assisted social and civic decision-making among digitally engaged youth in Egypt, Kuwait, and the United Arab Emirates. Methods A cross-sectional online survey was conducted with 1,023 respondents aged 18–35 recruited through purposive, non-probability sampling. Confirmatory factor analysis (CFA), structural equation modeling (SEM), multi-group CFA, and competing full- versus partial-mediation models evaluated measurement and structural relationships. Results The partially mediated model fit significantly better than the fully mediated model, Δχ2(5) = 55.66, p < 0.001. Institutional confidence (β = 0.303), AI literacy (β = 0.281), perceived usefulness (β = 0.242), and social influence (β = 0.107) were positively associated with trust in AI, and perceived risk was negatively associated (β = −0.106; all p < 0.001). Trust was positively associated with AI-assisted decision-making (β = 0.412, p < 0.001). Significant indirect associations through trust were observed for all five antecedents, while the direct perceived-risk path to AI-assisted decision-making was nonsignificant. Multi-group CFA supported metric and practical scalar measurement invariance across the three countries. Discussion The findings support a socio-technical account of AI trust in which technological, cognitive, institutional, and social conditions jointly relate to AI-assisted decision-making, with trust functioning as a central but not exclusive pathway. Given the cross-sectional, purposive design, findings are interpreted as associations rather than causal or nationally representative effects.

items.title: Uneven automation: comparing authorship anxiety and generative AI use among art and design undergraduate students
items.abstract: Art and design education expects students to develop a sense of authorship over original work, but generative AI (GenAI) complicates how students understand and claim that authorship. This study examined whether these experiences differ across creative fields through a mixed-methods design. The survey included 2,441 GenAI-using students from seven field categories at 33 art and design institutions in China and assessed authorship anxiety, creative agency, perceived usefulness, dependence on GenAI, and frequency of use. The quantitative analysis first examined variation across all seven categories and then compared fine art with the five applied design fields. Interview data from 22 survey participants were also examined thematically. The main findings include that (1) authorship anxiety did not differ significantly across the seven categories or between fine art and pooled design; the latter comparison met the equivalence criterion at ±d = 0.20, but not at tighter bounds; (2) clearer differences emerged in how students used GenAI. Compared with fine-art students, design students considered GenAI more useful and used it more frequently; (3) across the interviews, most students described authorship as retaining control over the creative idea while delegating parts of its execution to GenAI. Specifically, fine-art students often grounded authorship in embodied making and human imperfection, whereas design students placed greater emphasis on judgement, selection, and control. We call this pattern uneven automation: concern about authorship was broadly shared, but students in different fields responded to GenAI in different ways, potentially reflecting the varying labour-market pressures surrounding their disciplines.

items.title: Why so serious? Generative AI in Knowledge-Work from a Text-Workers’ Perspective
items.abstract: Generative AI (genAI) systems have become an integral part of scientific text-producing practice. They can conduct literature-related research, organize content and information, proofread text, and assist with writing itself. Above all, they are credited with reducing workload by taking on or taking over these routine tasks. Drawing on an internal, interdisciplinary KIT-ITAS project that deployed the genAI-supported research assistance system 'Undermind.ai', we demonstrate that the potential to reduce workload is offset by the need to reorganize basic scientific competencies in response to the changing workflow requirements of genAI-assisted knowledge work. GenAI systems produce texts that closely resemble stylistic conventions and appear both well-formed and plausible. However, the closer these texts adhere to researchers’ expectations, the more challenging it becomes to verify their content using established academic methods. This generates higher-order efforts that must be weighed against existing working standards for assessing text-based results. The constant validation and ongoing negotiation of plausibility with the system’s output, both during and beyond the writing process, places additional demands on researchers’ critical competence and judgement. Using genAI in knowledge work thus shifts the focus of familiar textual and intellectual labour practices and procedures away from independent creation and toward the verification of textual output, along with the corresponding demands on epistemic attention, responsibility, authorization, and authority.

items.title: A Comparison of the Effectiveness of AI-Assisted Learning versus Conventional Media for Children
items.abstract: This study examined the comparative effectiveness of artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted learning and conventional instructional media among fourth- and fifth-grade elementary school students. Although AI is increasingly promoted as a means of personalizing instruction, empirical evidence directly comparing AI-based and conventional approaches at the elementary level remains limited. A quasi-experimental Pretest-Posttest Control Group Design was employed, involving 42 students in an AI-assisted experimental group and 42 students in a conventionally taught control group drawn from intact classrooms within the same school. Learning effectiveness was operationalized through normalized gain (N-Gain) scores derived from pretest and posttest achievement tests previously established as valid and reliable. Because the experimental group's N-Gain scores departed from a normal distribution, between-group differences were examined using the Mann-Whitney U test, complemented by Cohen's d to estimate practical significance. Results showed that although the two groups began with statistically equivalent pretest scores, the experimental group achieved a significantly higher N-Gain (M = 0.40, medium category) than the control group (M = 0.26, low category), U = 1190.500, p = .006, with a medium effect size (d = 0.551). These findings indicate that AI-assisted learning produced greater and more consistent improvement than conventional media among elementary learners. The study contributes empirical evidence to the underrepresented area of AI-supported elementary education and offers practical guidance for teachers, curriculum developers, and policymakers integrating AI into classroom instruction.
