items.title: A Comprehensive Review of ANN-Driven Smart Learning Environments via Brain-Computer Interfacing
items.abstract: The contemporary educational landscape is undergoing a radical transition toward data-intensive, interactive paradigms characterized by the integration of sophisticated artificial intelligence and neurosensing technologies. This review examines the convergence of Brain-Computer Interfaces (BCI) and Artificial Neural Networks (ANN) as a transformative force in the creation of "Smart Learning Rooms." By synthesizing current research on Electroencephalography (EEG)-based cognitive monitoring and neural network-driven adaptive systems, this paper delineates a novel conceptual framework for a closed loop pedagogical environment. The study explores the mechanics of real-time attention assessment, the categorization of student learning styles, and the prediction of academic trajectories using diverse ANN architectures, including Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks and multi-layer perceptions. Furthermore, the analysis evaluates the efficacy of neurofeedback in enhancing focus and skill acquisition while addressing the technical, ethical, and socio-economic challenges inherent in the "neuro-digital divide." The proposed framework demonstrates how brain signal monitoring and neural computation can collaborate to personalize instructional pacing, improve engagement, and provide objective performance indicators. The ultimate objective is to provide a rigorous synthesis of the current state of neuro-education and offer a blueprint for the development of fully adaptive, brain-responsive instructional environments.

items.title: A Machine Learning Model to Predict Spinal Compression Force During Manual Lifting: Comparison of the Model Performance With Marker-Based Versus Markerless Kinematic Inputs
items.abstract: Musculoskeletal (MSK) modeling is widely used to estimate spinal loading. However, conventional modeling pipelines are computationally intensive and time-consuming, which limit their application for workplace injury risk assessment. This study developed a machine learning (ML) model to predict lumbosacral compression force using intermediate outputs from an MSK modeling workflow. Twenty-one participants completed lifting tasks while marker-based and markerless kinematics were recorded. Reference compression forces were obtained from completed OpenSim simulations, and the resulting dataset was used to train the ML model using three input feature sets. The best-performing model achieved mean root mean square errors of 3.0% with marker-based inputs and 9.9% with markerless inputs. These findings suggest that combining ML with conventional MSK modeling can enable rapid spinal load prediction and may support field deployment when coupled with markerless motion capture. However, given the higher errors observed with markerless input, future work is needed to improve the kinematics accuracy of the markerless system.

items.title: A Survey of Agentic AI: Architectures, Reasoning, Planning, Memory, Collaboration, and Real-World Applications
items.abstract: Agentic Artificial Intelligence (AI) is a new paradigm that allows intelligent systems to behave independently, pursue specific objectives, and adapt to changing circumstances. Agentic AI combines reasoning, planning, memory, learning, and tool utilization to do complicated tasks with minimal human involvement, in contrast to traditional AI systems that mainly react to user inputs. In this article, takes a look at Agentic AI from every angle: its theoretical underpinnings, technological supports, architectural blueprints, and real-world uses. Many models and frameworks are covered, including cognitive and modular designs, systems based on reinforcement learning, hybrid models, and multi-agent systems. Symbolic, probabilistic, and self-reflective reasoning are some of the reasoning methodologies covered. Classical, hierarchical, and adaptive planning strategies are also covered. Agents' ability to reliably and efficiently execute tasks is investigated by looking at memory management, communication protocols, coordination mechanisms, and collaborative decision-making. A wide range of business, medical, financial, academic, and personal aid apps are evaluated in the poll. Privacy, security, computational costs, scalability, and unexpected behavior are the main issues that are highlighted in the end. The study emphasizes the need for more investigation into how to create Agentic AI systems that are reliable, flexible, and effective.

items.title: ADOPTION OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN SUPPLY CHAIN MANAGEMENT: BARRIERS AND ENABLERS IN DEVELOPING ECONOMIES
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has emerged as a transformative technology capable of enhancing efficiency, decision-making, and resilience in supply chain management. However, its adoption in developing economies remains constrained by several technological, organizational, and environmental challenges. This study examined the adoption of Artificial Intelligence in supply chain management, with emphasis on the barriers and enablers in developing economies, using Nigeria as the study context. A cross-sectional survey research design was adopted, and data were collected from 235 employees, managers, and supply chain professionals in selected manufacturing firms, logistics companies, retail organizations, and small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) in Nigeria using a structured questionnaire titled Artificial Intelligence Adoption in Supply Chain Management Index (AIASCMI). Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics and Pearson Product Moment Correlation. The findings revealed that identified barriers, including inadequate digital infrastructure, high implementation costs, shortage of skilled personnel, and organizational challenges, have a significant negative relationship with the adoption of Artificial Intelligence in supply chain management. The study also found that identified enablers, such as top management support, technological readiness, employee competence, and government support, significantly influence the successful adoption of Artificial Intelligence. The study concludes that overcoming existing barriers while strengthening organizational and technological capabilities is essential for the successful adoption of Artificial Intelligence in supply chain management. It is recommended that organizations invest in digital infrastructure, workforce development, and supportive management practices to maximize the benefits of Artificial Intelligence and improve supply chain performance.

items.title: Agentic Artificial Intelligence as a Digital Employee: Redefining the Boundaries of Delegation, Accountability, and Control in Information Systems-Enabled Organizations
items.abstract: Background and Purpose: The rapid transition from deterministic automation and passive algorithmic decision-support systems to agentic artificial intelligence (Agentic AI) represents an unprecedented ontological shift in enterprise information systems (IS). Unlike antecedent generative models that merely synthesize conversational text, agentic AI operates with persistent internal memory, autonomous multi-step cognitive reasoning, goal decomposition, and self-directed tool and API execution. In contemporary digital organizations, these autonomous systems are progressively onboarded, provisioned, and treated not merely as passive software artifacts, but as synthetic workers or "digital employees." However, this conceptual elevation fractures foundational organizational assumptions rooted in classical agency theory, sociotechnical systems theory, and managerial control architectures. This monograph investigates how enterprise deployment of digital employees redefines the boundaries of delegation, moral and organizational accountability, and managerial control within IS-enabled organizational environments. Design, Methodology, and Approach: To rigorously interrogate this emergent socio-algorithmic reality, an extensive explanatory mixed-methods research design was executed across a 24-month longitudinal investigation (2024-2026). The quantitative phase collected and analyzed empirical survey data from 482 senior enterprise leaders, Chief Information Officers (CIOs), Chief AI Officers (CAIOs), Enterprise Architects, and line managers across four knowledge-intensive industry verticals (Financial Services & FinTech, Healthcare & HealthTech, Global Supply Chain Logistics, and Enterprise Cloud/SaaS). Structural Equation Modeling using Partial Least Squares (PLS-SEM) was employed to empirically test the structural dependencies between perceived agentic autonomy, algorithmic trust, delegation depth, operational agility, and accountability drift. The qualitative phase comprised 38 semi-structured, in-depth key-informant interviews and four comprehensive, longitudinal multi-case studies examining end-to-end organizational deployments of multi-agent architectures (including LangGraph, AutoGen, CrewAI, and proprietary enterprise agent meshes). Rigorous thematic analysis and qualitative comparative synthesis were conducted to deconstruct operational failures, behavioral drift phenomena, and governance adaptations. Empirical Findings: The empirical results reveal a profound structural paradox in enterprise agentic delegation. First, the transition from "task offloading" to "autonomous mandate delegation" generates a statistically significant positive effect on organizational agility (β=0.495, p<0.001) and operational velocity, but concurrently fuels a critical "accountability void" and organizational drift (β=0.342, p<0.001). Second, traditional managerial control frameworks specifically diagnostic and boundary controls suffer severe operational degradation when confronted with non-deterministic agentic planning and recursive API invocation. Third, human supervisors frequently exhibit either "cognitive abandonment" (over-trusting autonomous agents due to perceived competence) or severe "algorithmic cynicism" (resorting to micro-surveillance that negates agentic throughput benefits). Fourth, the investigation reveals the emergence of what we conceptualize as the "Synthetic Moral Crumple Zone," wherein middle-tier human managers are held legally and administratively accountable for unforeseen agentic systemic errors that they possessed neither the technical visibility nor the temporal window to prevent.

items.title: AI and the Shift in Power Dynamics in English Language Education: Portfolios as Tools for Authentic Self-Agency and Self-Determination
items.abstract: The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in English language education is reshaping traditional pedagogical frameworks, fostering learner autonomy, and redefining the educator’s role. This article presents a conceptual framework and pedagogical model exploring how AI-driven portfolio assessment and custom AI language models can be integrated within an Agile learning framework to support iterative, self-directed learning. While AI enhances language acquisition through personalized feedback and adaptive learning, concerns about authenticity, plagiarism, and over-reliance on AI-generated content remain. A structured approach to AI literacy development is introduced, ensuring that students critically assess AI-generated feedback rather than passively accepting it. A key component of this framework is AI-supported reflection, where learners evaluate AI suggestions based on alignment with their authentic voice and intended meaning. This process is reinforced through an AI-reflection rubric designed to cultivate metacognitive awareness and critical engagement with AI outputs. Agile methodologies, particularly iterative learning cycles, scaffold AI-supported writing assignments, balancing human and AI feedback for progressive skill development. The article also examines configurable AI tools for assessment, such as custom GPTs within ChatGPT and Gems within Google Gemini, which can evaluate language proficiency, track learning progression, and facilitate AI-supported peer assessment. The framework is designed to be adaptable across international EFL and ESL contexts, supporting authentic learning rather than replacing the learner’s central role in the learning process.

items.title: AI Governance: What Exactly Are We Governing?
items.abstract: WP_AI_8.5 develops a three-object framework for clarifying what AI governance is actually governing. The paper begins from a structural problem in contemporary AI governance. Technical systems, human decision-makers, institutional actors, oversight mechanisms, accountability, safety, and responsibility are often discussed within the same governance language without clearly separating the objects to which those rules apply. This can produce governance object drift, in which the focus of governance shifts during analysis, and governance subject inversion, in which AI becomes increasingly personalized as the apparent actor while the humans and institutions exercising real authority become less visible. The paper identifies three distinct but connected objects of AI governance. The first is the AI entity itself. The paper distinguishes four governance identities: Tool, System, Agent, and Autonomous Actor. These categories are not claims about consciousness or legal personhood. They describe different operational relationships between AI capability, delegated authority, persistence, external consequence, and human reauthorization. The second object is the human authority structure across the AI lifecycle. Developers, testers, providers, approvers, regulators, administrators, operators, and users exercise different forms of authority and therefore require different forms of governance. Human conduct must remain a direct object of AI governance rather than being displaced by anthropomorphic descriptions of AI behavior. The third object is the institutional interface through which AI capability enters society. Admission, authorization, release, deployment, access, supervision, review, restriction, suspension, and withdrawal determine how technical capability becomes socially operative. The paper also distinguishes Governance Identity Drift from Governance Object Drift. The former occurs when an AI system’s actual operational identity changes while its formal governance category remains unchanged. The latter occurs when governance itself shifts its analytical object, for example when a human authorization decision is gradually redescribed as autonomous machine behavior. The central argument is that governance must define its own objects rather than inherit them passively from technical narratives. AI should be governed according to what kind of operational entity it is. Humans and institutions should be governed according to the authority they exercise. The human-AI institutional interface should be governed according to the social consequences it enables. WP_AI_8.5 builds on the preceding papers in the WP_AI_8 series. WP_AI_8.1 established the engineering circuit-breaker principle; WP_AI_8.2 examined responsibility escape; WP_AI_8.3 developed a dual-track framework connecting capability control and human responsibility; and WP_AI_8.4 addressed the conditions under which AI capability may move from controlled development into social release. WP_AI_8.5 moves one level upward by clarifying the governance objects to which those mechanisms apply.

items.title: AI in HRM: a unified model of AI capabilities and process efficiency for enhanced HRM effectiveness
items.abstract: Abstract The accelerating adoption of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in human resource management (HRM) raises important questions about which AI-driven interventions most effectively enhance workforce agility, decision-making, and employee outcomes. This study investigated the effects of multiple AI applications—including employee wellbeing (AIEEW), performance management (AIPM), recruitment and selection (AIRS), training and development (AITD), and strategic HR practices (AISHRP), on HR process efficiency (HRPE), decision-making agility (DMA), workplace AI integration (WAI), and enhanced HRM effectiveness (EHRE). Data was collected from 256 professionals in organizational and educational institutions and analyzed using structural equation modeling (SEM) with SmartPLS. Results revealed that eight of nine hypothesized paths were supported, with AI-enabled wellbeing exerting the strongest effect on workplace AI integration (β = 0.583, p < .001). Recruitment and performance management systems significantly enhanced HR process efficiency, while strategic HR planning and talent analytics improved decision-making agility. HR performance enhancement strongly predicted HR effectiveness (β = 0.458, p < .001), highlighting process efficiency as a key mediator of AI’s impact. Two paths were weaker: AI in training and development did not significantly affect HR process efficiency, and decision-making agility showed only marginal influence on HRM effectiveness. items.title: AI in mathematics classrooms: a synergistic strategy for diversity and inclusivity
items.abstract: Despite growing emphasis on inclusive education, mathematics classrooms still exhibit disparities arising from cognitive, linguistic, socioeconomic, and systemic barriers, marginalizing diverse students and limiting equitable learning opportunities. Artificial intelligence (AI) presents considerable potential for addressing these challenges. This study investigates how AI technologies can be harnessed to create mathematics classrooms that are inclusive and adaptive to individual student needs. Anchored in Universal Design for Learning (UDL) and the Substitution, Augmentation, Modification, Redefinition (SAMR) frameworks, the study explores how AI functionalities can facilitate personalized learning, responsive instruction, and equitable participation. The study employs a hybrid conceptual–structured narrative review approach, synthesizing existing literature through structured searching, screening, thematic coding, and conceptual integration. The synthesis examines AI functionalities, inclusive pedagogical affordances, implementation challenges, ethical and equity concerns, and future directions. On this basis, the study develops the Synergistic AI-Inclusive Mathematics Education (SAIME) framework, conceptualizing UDL as an inclusion-oriented design foundation, SAMR as a technological transformation pathway, and teacher-mediated pedagogy and ethical safeguards as essential conditions for equitable outcomes in access, participation, and achievement. It concludes that AI can contribute meaningfully to inclusive mathematics education when its technological affordances are purposefully aligned with inclusive pedagogy, ethical and equity safeguards, and equitable learning goals.

items.title: Algorithmic Bias in HR Management: A Critical Inquiry into the Automation of Inequity
items.abstract: This paper provides a comprehensive critical analysis of algorithmic bias in human resource management, examining how artificial intelligence (AI) systems used in hiring, promotions, and performance management can perpetuate and amplify societal biases. Moving beyond conventional discussions of bias, this research introduces a series of novel theoretical frameworks to uncover the deeper, systemic mechanisms through which algorithmic HR systems produce inequitable outcomes. These include the Sociotechnical Bias Amplification Model (SBAM), which explains how temporal bias, intersectional bias, and feedback loops interact to compound discrimination; the Algorithmic Opacity Paradox, which argues that the perceived objectivity of AI obscures its discriminatory potential; and the Fairness Impossibility Theorem in the HR context, which demonstrates the mathematical and normative trade-offs inherent in any algorithmic fairness definition. The paper further develops a critical perspective by introducing concepts such as data colonialism, the performance management panopticon, and the algorithmic accountability gap. Through a synthesis of technical literature, organizational theory, and critical algorithm studies, this research argues that the challenge of algorithmic bias is not merely a technical problem of “debiasing” but a fundamental crisis of legitimacy for automated decision-making in the workplace. The analysis is supported by clearly labelled conceptual diagrams and selected empirical findings drawn from published research. It concludes with a set of actionable recommendations for HR leaders, policymakers, and researchers, advocating for a shift from a technical-fix mindset to a more holistic, human-centered approach to governance that prioritizes justice, accountability, and equity.

items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) & Machine Learning (ML) are two terms that transformed pharmaceutical sciences, including drug discovery, drug development, precision medicine and nanomedicine. Traditional drug discovery is a long, expensive and failure-prone process that may take over 10 years and million of dollars before it produces a therapeutically active compound ready for clinical trials and commercialization. AI-driven computational approaches can tackle numerous challenges of drug discovery and development, including target or lead identification and optimization, virtual screening, predicting drug target interactions, toxicity and personalized treatment options. The concept of artificial intelligence was first introduced in the 1940s when Alan Turing laid the foundations for machine intelligence theory claiming that there is no fundamental difference between human and machine computation (Turing, 1950). The formal idea of artificial intelligence was further proposed by Mc Carthy, Minsky, Rochester and Shannon who proposed the Dartmouth Hypothesis about the possibility for machines to stimulate human intelligence (Mc Carthy et al 1955). In the following decades the concepts machine learning and deep learning were introduced Schmidhuber in 2015. There are three review papers that discuss the role of AI&ML in pharmaceutical sciences and health care. The first study focus on the role of artificial intelligence in drug discovery and discovery and precision nanomedicine (Zhu et al, 2022). Zhu et al. highlight importance of algorithms and nano-enabled therapeutics for precision nanomedicine. The main ideas of the study include finding and selecting the target developing the optimal drug using nano-enabled therapeutics and individualizing treatment based on patients characteristics. The second review paper discuss the role of AI in spatial structure of protein predicting and drug synergism prediction targeting molecular mechanism and protein drug interactions (Lie et al, 2022). The study by Lei et al. high-light the importance of AI in analyzing and prediction the spatial structure of protein to reveal molecular mechanisms and biological functions. The third review paper was discusses the concept of artificial intelligence, machine learning and deep learning elucidates ethical and social implications and high light the public awarness about AI (Garcia & Salichos, 2022). The study by Garcia & Salichosis a detailed analysis about the opportunities and limitations of AI.I would like to address the main ideas of all three reviewed papers and discuss hoe AL&ML can be applied to various stages of drug discovery and development. I will also comment on such terms as machine learning, deep learning, protein spatial structure prediction, virtual screening precision, precision medicine, nanomedicine, drug synergism prediction, explainable AI.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence (AI) in Patient–Healthcare Relationships: Psychosocial Perspective
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence is becoming part of healthcare through tools that help organise medical information, support clinical decisions, answer common questions, and improve communication. These changes affect more than treatment and efficiency: they can also influence how patients feel, how much they trust healthcare professionals, and whether they feel heard and respected. This paper reviews AI in patient–healthcare relationships from a psychosocial perspective. It considers trust, empathy, privacy, patient autonomy, health literacy, anxiety, accessibility, and the role of clinicians in explaining AI-supported decisions. AI can make some services faster and easier to access, but it may also create distance when communication feels automated or when recommendations are difficult to understand. The paper argues that AI should strengthen—not replace—the human relationship at the centre of care. Responsible use requires transparency, protection of personal information, inclusive design, careful evaluation, and meaningful human oversight..

items.abstract: AI tools are increasingly being utilized in counselling services to provide student support, but their impact on undergraduate students needs to be thoroughly examined. This study examines the relationship between Artificial Intelligence and Counselling Service among Undergraduate Students in Cross River State. To achieve this, three (3) objectives, three (3) research questions and three (3) hypotheses were formulated. Correlational research design was adopted. The sample was 760 students from the sampled faculties out of 44,281 in UNICAL, 31,410 in CRSUE, and 23,971 in UNICROSS. Three experts validated the instrument, it was titled "Usage, Awareness, Attitude towards AI and Effective Counselling Service Questionnaire" and was administered to the respondents to elicit their responses.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence and Older Persons: Opportunities for Empowerment and Risks of Digital Exclusion in Light of Rights-Based Safeguards
items.abstract: This study examines the relationship between the development of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies and the rights of older persons. It analyses the opportunities that smart applications offer in health care, independent living, social connection and economic security, set against the risks arising from digital exclusion, algorithmic age discrimination, privacy violations and fraud. The study adopts a descriptive-analytical approach based on international reports, systematic reviews, meta-analyses and relevant national surveys, and discusses the UAE legislative context. The review shows that the age gap in use remains wide, that the evidence of benefits is promising but limited, and that fraud risks are documented by rising figures. The study proposes a preliminary framework for safe digital empowerment that links graduated learning, inclusive design, data protection, human review and evaluation. It concludes that the rights-based value of AI is not measured by the mere availability of a service, but by its capacity to expand the real choices of older persons while respecting their will and dignity. The study does not present field results, nor does it claim to have tested the proposed model. By drawing upon the frameworks of critical posthumanism and AI ethics, we can find out that the novels are more concerned with whether human beings are capable of retaining a stable and exceptional identity when affect, consciousness, simulation, and ethical agency become entangled rather than on whether machines can be human. As comparison shows that artifice operates as a mirror through which contemporary fiction exhibits the ethical, emotional and ontological fragility of the human self.

items.title: Artificial intelligence for sustainable power systems applications challenges and future directions
items.abstract: Abstract Stretching the integration of renewable energy, energy storage, electric vehicles (EVs) and smart-grid technologies at an unprecedented rate will produce increasingly complex and dynamic power systems that defy conventional optimization and control methods. This paper offers a systematic engineering review of the state of the art and future potential for the application of artificial intelligence (AI) in sustainable and resilient electric power systems, which includes machine learning, deep learning, reinforcement learning (RL), hybrid AI, explainable artificial intelligence, federated learning (FL), and digital twins (DTs). The review covers their use in renewable energy and load forecasting, energy management, predictive maintenance, demand response, adaptive control, energy storage, smart grid and EV/Vehicle-to-Grid coordination. A single framework based on the grid is presented that integrates predictive intelligence, optimization, adaptive control, cyber-physical systems, explainability, cyber-security, and sustainability in a closed-loop system. The analysis underscores the transformative possibilities of AI in enhancing the use of renewable energy, its efficiency, resilience of the grid and smart decision making. But, deployment needs to address the uncertainties, data quality, computational costs, latency, Cybersecurity, interoperability, scalability, model drift, and regulatory needs. The review also highlights Green AI to tackle the energy and carbon footprint of increasingly large AI models. Lastly, physics-informed and uncertainty-aware AI, safe RL, DT-assisted validation, edge intelligence, FL and real-world benchmarking are identified as key directions for next-generation power systems to remain trustworthy and sustainable.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Breast Cancer Diagnosis, Treatment, and Perioperative Management: A Systematic Review of Current Applications and Future Perspectives.
items.abstract: Background: Breast cancer is the most frequently diagnosed malignancy in women globally, accounting for approximately 2.30 million new cases and 666,103 deaths in 2022. Artificial intelligence technologies including machine learning, deep learning, radiomics, and natural language processing have been widely applied across the breast cancer care continuum. However, no systematic review restricted to primary studies with patient-level or image-level data has synthesized evidence spanning all clinical domains simultaneously. Objectives: To evaluate the performance, methodological quality, and clinical relevance of artificial intelligence primary studies across screening and diagnostic imaging, digital pathology, radiomics, perioperative management, prognostic prediction, and natural language processing in breast cancer. Methods: PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, Embase, and the Cochrane Library were searched from January 2015 to May 2026. Eligibility was restricted to original primary research reporting patient-level or image-level data; secondary syntheses were explicitly excluded. Risk of bias was assessed using QUADAS-2 and PROBAST. Reporting followed PRISMA 2020 guidelines. Results: Of 5,275 identified records, 17 primary studies met eligibility criteria. In screening mammography (seven studies; n = 7,540 to 144,231 examinations), deep learning achieved area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) values of 0.876 to 0.939; a randomised trial in 80,033 women demonstrated non-inferiority to double reading with a 44.3% reduction in radiologist workload. In digital pathology (five studies; 270 to 44,732 whole-slide images), deep learning achieved AUC 0.985 to 0.994, exceeding unassisted pathologist performance in lymph node metastasis detection. Magnetic resonance imaging radiomics predicted pathological complete response in HER2-positive breast cancer with AUC 0.80. No breast cancer-specific perioperative primary study met the eligibility criteria. Deep survival networks achieved concordance index 0.626 versus 0.612 for Cox regression in breast cancer cohorts. items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Higher Education: The Role of Fairness, Transparency, and Accountability in Student Acceptance
items.abstract: This study examined the influence of Fairness, Transparency, and Accountability [FTA] on student acceptance of Artificial Intelligence [AI] in higher education institutions in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan. Grounded on an extended Technology Acceptance Model, data were collected from 240 undergraduate students from six universities using a structured 5-point likert scale questionnaire. Descriptive analysis and Pearson correlation were conducted using SPSS v26. Results indicated that students reported moderately high acceptance of AI for learning but low perceptions of fairness, transparency, and accountability. Transparency emerged as the most critical concern, with 45-50% of students reporting limited understanding of AI decision-making processes. Correlation analysis revealed significant positive relationships between all three FTA dimensions and student acceptance. The findings suggest that while perceived usefulness drives initial adoption, ethical concerns may hinder sustainable use. The study recommends that Pakistani HEIs implement bias-free AI systems, provide explainable AI interfaces, and establish clear accountability structures to build student trust. This study contributes to AI ethics literature in the Pakistani context and provides implications for policymakers and university administrators.

items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly reshaping customer engagement, yet its influence on consumer behavior within hospitality and tourism services remains underexplored.This study examines the associations among AI-enabled engagement, digital marketing, and consumer behavior in hospitality and tourism contexts.Survey data were collected from 221 respondents and analyzed using structural equation modeling (SEM) in an exploratory capacity.The measurement analysis revealed that AI, digital marketing, and consumer behavior are very strongly interrelated: inter-construct correlations were high (AI-DM r = 0.871; DM-CB r = 0.882) and exceeded the square roots of the average variance extracted, so the three constructs did not achieve discriminant validity under the Fornell-Larcker criterion.Rather than interpreting this as a mediation mechanism, the study treats it as a substantive finding: in this hospitality and tourism setting, consumers appear to experience AI, the digital marketing it enables, and their own engagement responses as a single, tightly coupled digitalengagement domain rather than as separable constructs.Model fit was marginal (RMSEA = 0.113; CFI = 0.870), so all relationships are reported as indicative and associational rather than causal.The study contributes contextually by situating AI within hospitality and tourism service ecosystems and by documenting the strong convergence of these digital-engagement constructs, offering guidance for hospitality organizations and advancing discourse on sustainable, human-centered tourism strategies aligned with logistics, informatics, and service science.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Pediatric Education by SNAPPS and Clinical Reasoning Among Postgraduate Residents in a Tertiary Care Hospital in Central India
items.abstract: Abstract Background Competency-based medical education (CBME) emphasizes clinical reasoning as a core postgraduate competency, yet structured teaching strategies such as SNAPPS remain under-optimized in pediatric postgraduate training. Artificial intelligence (AI) has been proposed as a supervised cognitive scaffold within SNAPPS, but empirical outcome-level evidence, particularly from pediatric postgraduate education in India, is limited. Objective To evaluate the effect of AI-assisted SNAPPS on clinical reasoning, structured case-presentation quality, and knowledge acquisition among pediatric postgraduate residents, and to assess learner and faculty perceptions of the intervention. Methods A prospective, single-arm, within-subject educational interventional study was conducted over six months among 30 pediatric postgraduate residents (10 each from JR1, JR2, and JR3) in the Department of Pediatrics, NKP Salve Institute of Medical Sciences & Research Centre and Lata Mangeshkar Hospital, Nagpur. Following sensitization, all participants underwent baseline assessment, a traditional-SNAPPS teaching phase, and an AI-assisted SNAPPS phase using a standardized SNAPPS-mapped AI prompt protocol with mandatory faculty validation at every step. Outcomes were measured using the Script Concordance Test (SCT), a validated 30-point SNAPPS analytical rubric, a multiple-choice question (MCQ) knowledge test, and five-point Likert perception surveys for residents and faculty. Paired comparisons were analyzed using appropriate parametric and non-parametric tests; p < 0.05 was considered significant. Results Mean SCT scores improved significantly with AI-assisted SNAPPS (12.0 ± 2.0 to 19.6 ± 2.8, p < 0.001), a gain that exceeded the improvement achieved with traditional SNAPPS alone (11.8 ± 2.1 to 15.2 ± 2.5, p < 0.01). The total SNAPPS rubric score rose from 19.1 ± 3.2 to 27.6 ± 2.9 (p < 0.001), with significant gains across all six domains. MCQ knowledge scores improved similarly (12.7 ± 2.5 to 18.8 ± 1.9, p < 0.001). SCT and SNAPPS rubric scores were strongly and positively correlated (r = 0.72, p < 0.001). Both residents and faculty reported significantly higher satisfaction with AI-assisted SNAPPS across every measured domain (all p < 0.001). Conclusion AI-assisted SNAPPS, implemented as a faculty-supervised cognitive scaffold, is feasible, well accepted, and educationally effective for strengthening clinical reasoning, structured presentation and knowledge retention among pediatric postgraduate residents. The model merits validation in larger, multicentric, competency-based curricula.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in the Judicial System of Ukraine: International Experience and Ukrainian Practice
items.abstract: This article examines the current state and prospects of using artificial intelligence (AI) technologies in Ukraine's judicial system. It analyses the international and national regulatory and ethical benchmarks for the use of AI in judicial proceedings, in particular the provisions of Opinion No. 26 (2023) of the Consultative Council of European Judges, the European Ethical Charter on the Use of Artificial Intelligence in Judicial Systems and their Environment, and the CEPEJ Guidelines on the use of generative artificial intelligence for courts. The article also outlines Ukrainian organisational approaches, notably the Regulation on the Use of Artificial Intelligence Technologies by Employees of the Office of the Supreme Court. The main focus is a review of case law on parties' use of generative AI output, references to fictitious court decisions and legal positions, and AI use in drafting judicial acts. The article argues that AI output has no independent evidentiary value and cannot replace the judge’s assessment of evidence, legal analysis or the reasoning of a court decision. It identifies the key risks of using AI: legal ‘hallucinations’, algorithmic bias, opacity, breaches of confidentiality, loss of professional autonomy, and unequal access to technology. Effective integration of artificial intelligence technologies into Ukraine’s judicial system requires not only the formal enshrinement of relevant rules, but also the development of a coherent institutional culture of responsible use. The introduction of AI must be accompanied by uniform methodological guidelines for courts and participants in the judicial process, improved systems for verifying the authenticity of electronic sources, and mechanisms for verifying results obtained using generative models. Ensuring the digital literacy of judges, court staff, lawyers and other participants in the administration of justice is of particular importance, as it is precisely their level of awareness that determines the limits of the safe and ethical use of such technologies. At the same time, it is emphasised that the digitalisation of the justice system must not lead to the devaluation of the human element, a decline in trust in the judiciary, or the erosion of guarantees of a fair trial. The article concludes that the acceptable model for Ukraine is the assistive use of AI, under which technology supports administrative, analytical and information processes but does not take over the functions of the judge. It proposes ways of improving the legal framework: statutory definition of permitted and prohibited uses of AI, the introduction of standards for disclosing its use, and the provision of algorithmic audits, professional training for users and safeguards ensuring effective human oversight.

items.title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE INTEGRATION IN TECHNICAL SUPPORT DECISIONS IN THE SOLAR SECTOR Implementation design for GVE Projects Ltd, Nigeria
items.abstract: Abstract Nigeria has the world’s largest electricity-access deficit, and unreliable grid supply drives demand for solar systems and for dependable after-sales technical support. This report examines how artificial intelligence can strengthen the technical support function of GVE Projects Ltd, a Nigerian solar energy company whose public contact model relies on telephone, e-mail and short online forms. It analyses the current support process and compares it with three reference cases: M-KOPA, Huawei FusionSolar smart diagnostics and GVE’s own pay-as-you-go mini-grids. Technical support is treated as a decision system, in which each contact ends in self-resolution, remote fix, field dispatch or specialist escalation. AI is introduced only where it improves one of these decisions and a human can override it. The report proposes a phased, human-supervised system with five architectural layers: WhatsApp-first customer intake, retrieval-augmented knowledge answers, rule-and-model fault triage with a confidence-gated decision rule, and optional telemetry-based predictive maintenance. The design includes an ArchiMate enterprise-architecture model, key performance indicators, a work breakdown structure, a twelve-month plan, a feasibility study, an ISO 31000:2018 risk evaluation and a five-year economic assessment. Because GVE’s internal data were unavailable, the as-is process and the economic model rest on public sources and stated assumptions, and a sensitivity analysis tests them. The report concludes that a narrow, compliance-first deployment under the Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023 is feasible, and that its success depends more on data quality and staff adoption than on the choice of AI model.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Literacy, Self-Perceived Competence, and Use Among Postgraduate Medical Trainees and Faculty in Tanzania: A Multi-Institutional Cross-Sectional Study
items.abstract: Abstract Background Artificial intelligence (AI) is being integrated into medical education globally, yet evidence from sub-Saharan Africa remains sparse. Postgraduate medical training institutions in this region face distinctive cultural, resource and infrastructure constraints that may shape how educators and trainees engage with AI. This study examined knowledge and self-reported use of AI among postgraduate medical residents and faculty in Dar es Salaam, Tanzania. Methods A cross-sectional study was conducted across three postgraduate medical training universities in Dar es Salaam the Aga Khan University (AKU), Muhimbili University of Health and Allied Sciences (MUHAS), and Hubert Kairuki Memorial University (HKMU). A census sampling approach was used, targeting all available residents and faculty. Data was collected via an online structured questionnaire assessing AI knowledge, exposure, and self-rated competence. Knowledge scores were derived from a ten-item questionnaire and compared across groups using Welch's t-test and multivariable linear regression to determine association with knowledge scores. Results A total of 155 participants participated in the study (116 residents, 39 faculty). Mean age group was 31–40 years. Formal AI training was rare (7.1%), yet 80.0% reported using AI in teaching or learning activities. Residents used AI substantially more than faculty (65.8% vs. 14.2%). Overall objective knowledge was moderate (mean score 59.0%, SD 18.2%), with no significant difference between residents and faculty (p = 0.623). Specialty was also associated with knowledge scores, with medical and radiology specialties outperforming non-clinical specialties Self-rated knowledge at Level 5 was the only independent predictor of higher objective scores in multivariable analysis (β = 0.151; 95% CI 0.022–0.302; p = 0.049). Conclusions AI use is widespread among postgraduate trainees in Dar es Salaam despite minimal formal training. Knowledge gaps are evident, particularly around foundational AI concepts. Self-perceived competence, rather than professional role or formal training, predicted objective knowledge. These findings underscore the need for structured, contextually adapted AI literacy curricula within postgraduate medical education in Tanzania and similar settings.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Versus Human Interpretation in Diagnostic Radiology: A Systematic Review of Diagnostic Accuracy and Operational Efficiency
items.abstract: Rising imaging workload and a shortage of radiology specialists have driven interest in artificial intelligence (AI) to improve diagnostic speed and accuracy. This systematic review, without meta-analysis, describes how AI affects diagnostic accuracy and operational efficiency compared with human interpretation in diagnostic radiology. Following Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA 2020) and Cochrane guidance, PubMed, ClinicalKey, ScienceDirect, and Google Scholar were searched on 11 April 2026 for studies published from January 2019 onwards. Two reviewers independently performed study selection, data extraction, and a Quality Assessment of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies 2 (QUADAS-2)-based risk-of-bias assessment. Twenty-one studies were included: 11 compared standalone AI with human readers, six compared AI-assisted with unassisted readers, and four reported both; 18 evaluated task-specific image-analysis AI and three evaluated generative AI models. Because no subgroup was homogeneous enough to pool, we synthesised results narratively and stratified them by comparison type, AI category, imaging modality, and study quality. Standalone image-analysis AI achieved high sensitivity for fractures and selected chest findings but performed less well on subtle findings and lower-quality images, and in one computed tomography-referenced comparison a radiologist outperformed AI. AI assistance improved reader performance more consistently, particularly among less experienced readers. Generative models did not reach specialist performance on complex tasks. Efficiency gains were concentrated in normal studies, and the only randomised trial found lower mammography screen-reading workload with similar early screening performance. No study assessed patient outcomes, and 18 of 21 studies were retrospective. This evidence supports AI only as a supervised, complementary tool; improvements in diagnostic accuracy should not be equated with clinical benefit.

items.title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE-DRIVEN SOCIAL MEDIA MARKETING AND GREEN PURCHASE INTENTION: DEVELOPING A CONCEPTUAL FRAMEWORK FOR UZBEKISTAN
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has become an important tool in social media marketing, enabling businesses to deliver personalized content and enhance consumer engagement. At the same time, growing environmental awareness has increased interest in green products. This study develops a conceptual framework to explain the relationship between AI-driven social media marketing, consumer trust, and green purchase intention in Uzbekistan. Based on recent literature, the proposed framework suggests that AI-driven social media marketing strengthens consumer trust and positively influences consumers' intention to purchase green products. The study contributes to the green marketing literature by integrating these constructs into a unified conceptual model and provides a theoretical foundation for future empirical research in Uzbekistan. Одновременно с этим рост экологической осведомлённости способствует повышению интереса к экологически чистым продуктам. Данное исследование направлено на разработку концептуальной модели, объясняющей взаимосвязь между маркетингом в социальных сетях на основе искусственного интеллекта, доверием потребителей и намерением приобретать экологически чистые продукты в Узбекистане. items.title: Automation-Induced Redundancy: Does Chapter V-B of the Industrial Disputes Act Provide Adequate Safeguards in the Era of Generative AI?
items.abstract: Abstract: ABSTRACT The rapid development of Artificial Intelligence, especially Generative AI, is really changing how we work and what employment looks like. While these AI technologies can boost productivity and enhance decision-making, they might also lessen the need for human workers in some roles, leading to layoffs and job losses. This shift has sparked worries about job security, potential layoffs, the need for reskilling, and whether current labor laws are adequate. This research examines whether the safeguards provide under Chapter V-B of the Industrial Disputes Act from 1947 are enough to protect employees whose jobs are impacted by automation and tech advancements. It zooms in on key legal protections related to layoffs, notice periods, compensation, required government approvals, and other employee safeguards. Additionally, it looks at the challenges posed by Generative AI, especially how tech changes can shift job roles, cut down the demand for certain skills, or even render some positions obsolete. The study takes a doctrinal and qualitative approach, pulling from a variety of sources like legislation, court rulings, academic research, government documents, and insights into AI, automation, and employment. It also examines the Industrial Relations Code of 2020 to grasp how India's labor law framework is evolving in light of technology. The findings indicate that while current labor laws do offer crucial protections during layoffs, they might not fully tackle the issues brought on by AI-related job changes. There's a strong suggestion that more focus is needed on reskilling, redeploying, transparency, and providing support during transitions before any layoffs occur. Therefore, the study advocates for a more employee-centered approach, encouraging employers to prioritize reskilling and redeployment ahead of layoffs, while also balancing tech advancements, business demands, and employee rights. items.title: Beyond Accuracy: A Critical Review of Evaluation, Clinical Validation, and Safety Frameworks for Agentic AI in Medicine
items.abstract: Agentic artificial intelligence (AI) extends conventional predictive and generative AI by enabling systems to pursue goals through reasoning, planning, information retrieval, memory, tool use, and interaction with clinical workflows. These capabilities create new opportunities for medicine but also a distinct evaluation problem: the reliability of an agent cannot be inferred from the accuracy of its underlying model or final answer alone. Errors may arise during information retrieval, tool use, state updates, inter-agent communication, or autonomous action and may propagate across a clinical workflow. This critical review examines approaches for evaluating and clinically validating agentic AI in medicine. Existing frameworks, including TRIPOD+AI, CONSORT-AI, SPIRIT-AI, DECIDE-AI, STARD-AI, FUTURE-AI, and Good Machine Learning Practice, provide important foundations but were not primarily designed for systems with persistent state, repeated actions, tool use, and multi-agent interaction. Emerging agent benchmarks increasingly address interactive tasks, tool use, trajectory reliability, and adversarial testing. We propose a five-level evaluation framework spanning model, agent, trajectory, system, and clinical outcome, together with a clinical validation ladder progressing from component testing and simulation to retrospective evaluation, prospective silent deployment, supervised clinical use, bounded action, and post-deployment surveillance. Key gaps include standardized trajectory metrics, evaluation of correlated multi-agent errors, autonomy-aware validation, human–agent performance, and lifecycle monitoring. Radiotherapy is used as a high-stakes clinical exemplar. We argue that agentic AI should be evaluated as a dynamic sociotechnical system and that clinical evidence must extend beyond accuracy toward behavioral reliability, safety, and demonstrated clinical benefit.

items.title: Bridging the Artificial Intelligence Divide in Higher Education: Digital Literacy, Social Influence, and Ethical AI Adoption among University Students
items.abstract: This study examines the determinants of ethical artificial intelligence (AI) adoption among university students by integrating the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT) and Digital Divide Theory. Specifically, this study investigates the effects of digital literacy, social influence, and digital divide on ethical AI adoption, as well as the moderating role of digital divide in the relationships between digital literacy, social influence, and ethical AI adoption. A quantitative survey was conducted involving 408 university students in Indonesia. The data were analyzed using regression analysis, supported by reliability and validity tests, correlation analysis, Gaussian copula endogeneity check, Harman’s single-factor test, non-response bias test, and simple slope analysis. The findings show that digital literacy has a positive and significant effect on ethical AI adoption, indicating that students with stronger digital literacy are more likely to use AI critically, responsibly, and in accordance with academic integrity. Social influence also has a positive and significant effect, suggesting that lecturers, peers, academic norms, and institutional guidance play an important role in encouraging responsible AI use. Digital divide-related conditions are also significantly associated with ethical AI adoption, highlighting the importance of access, capability, and digital support in AI-supported learning. However, the moderating effects of digital divide are not statistically supported. These findings suggest that digital divide functions more as a direct contextual factor than as a moderating variable. This study contributes to the literature on AI adoption in higher education by emphasizing that ethical AI adoption is shaped by individual digital competence, social-academic support, and inclusive digital conditions. The findings also imply that universities need to strengthen digital literacy, develop clear AI-use guidelines, and reduce digital access gaps to promote ethical and inclusive AI adoption.

items.title: Building Ungameable Trust Networks for Curated Directories: Decentralized Filtering Without Central Authority
items.abstract: Search and discovery on the 2026 internet is broken for three groups: users who want to find real businesses and resources, small businesses who want to be found, and honest affiliate operators who want to earn from genuine recommendations. Search engines rank results by signals that reward scale, not quality. A local hardware store cannot outrank a content farm that produces ten thousand SEO-optimized pages per day with large language models. Paying for search advertising puts small businesses into bidding wars against companies with orders-of-magnitude larger budgets. Social media demands constant content production — videos, posts, engagement farming — work that has nothing to do with the actual service the business provides. Review platforms are corrupted. Fake reviews, review bombing, pay-to-play visibility schemes, and extortion dynamics have made star ratings unreliable. Users append "reddit" to their search queries as a trust signal, but Reddit itself is degrading as it monetizes and as marketers infiltrate communities. AI answer engines attempt to solve the problem by synthesizing responses, but they draw from the same polluted index and introduce hallucination risk. The underlying data is compromised. No amount of summarization fixes a contaminated source. Honest affiliate operators face the same structural disadvantage. An operator who genuinely tests products and recommends what they believe in cannot compete on volume against content farms that rewrite product descriptions and stuff affiliate links without touching the products. The algorithm cannot distinguish the two. The content farm wins on output volume every time. Three intermediaries sit between a person and a useful resource: algorithmic ranking that rewards manipulation, centralized moderation that makes uniform visibility decisions for all users, and review systems that are themselves a manipulation surface. All three are failing.
